query: How can we formally derive and present appendix proofs mapping the directional frontier p* to the Lerner index and to consumer surplus changes under two demand primitives (CES/constant elasticity and logit/random-coefficients)?

response.query: How can we formally derive and present appendix proofs mapping the directional frontier p* to the Lerner index and to consumer surplus changes under two demand primitives (CES/constant elasticity and logit/random-coefficients)?
response.answer: The directional frontier p* maps to the Lerner index and consumer surplus changes via the elasticity of demand under CES and logit models. Consumer surplus is linked to the inverse demand function, and its changes depend on elasticity variations.

results.content: # Why Consumer Surplus is Negative the Integral of the Demand Function. I’ve learned that, up to a constant, consumer surplus is the integral of the demand function. It’s negative the integral of the demand function. The reason has to do with the fact that what we call the demand function–that which translates price into quantity–is not what we draw on a graph. Thanks to Alfred Marshall, the custom is to draw the *inverse* demand function, with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis. To show formally that consumer surplus is the negative of the integral of demand (or that demand is negative the derivative of consumer surplus), one can use the rule for integrating inverses. * *Q = D(P)* be the demand function,. If one is working with discrete choice models (logit, nested logit, conditional logit, etc.) and wishes to derive the expression for consumer surplus, one might do so by recalling two things:. 1. The functional form of consumer surplus is the log of the denominator of the discrete choice probability model, which is also the demand function. That is, consumer surplus has a log-sum of exponentials form. 2. The derivative of consumer surplus is negative the demand function, i.e. the discrete choice model. results.title: How is consumer surplus affected by the elasticity of a demand curve? - Quora
results.content: Consumer surplus is the difference between value a consumer attaches to a product i.e the maximum price a consumer is willing to pay (the height of the demand curve) and the price he actually pays (market price). For a product with perfectly elastic demand curve (demand curve is completely horizontal), the maximum price consumer is willing to pay exactly equals the market price (any attempt to charge a higher price than the market price, in case of a perfectly elastic demand curve, results in zero sales), thus consumer surplus is zero. For a product with perfectly elastic demand curve (demand curve is completely horizontal), the maximum price consumer is willing to pay exactly equals the market price (any attempt to charge a higher price than the market price, in case of a perfectly elastic demand curve, results in zero sales), thus consumer surplus is zero. In case of a perfectly inelastic demand (completely vertical demand curve), a consumer is willing to pay infinite price for the same quantity (it is true only theoretically), thus the consumer surplus is also infinite. Title: Semi-nonparametric estimation of random coefficients logit model for aggregate demand
IDEAS home Printed from https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/econom/v235y2023i2p2245-2265.html. # Semi-nonparametric estimation of random coefficients logit model for aggregate demand. In this paper, we propose a two-step semi-nonparametric estimator for the widely used random coefficients logit demand model. The approach applies to the same setup as Berry et al. The second step uncovers the distribution of the random coefficient via a sieve minimum distance or GMM procedure. We show identification and derive the asymptotic properties of the estimator in a large market environment. results.content: # Monopoly price discrimination with constant elasticity demand. This paper presents new results on the welfare effects of third-degree price discrimination under constant elasticity demand. We show that when both the share of the strong market under uniform pricing and the elasticity difference between markets are high enough, then price discrimination not only can increase social welfare but also consumer surplus.
